A small, fully reproducible analysis of a classroom Stroop-task dataset,
used to teach an open and reproducible data analysis workflow. Students in
an introductory psychology course named colors in congruent trials (e.g.,
the word "red" printed in red) and incongruent trials (e.g., "red" printed
in green); the time to name all words in each block was self-reported in
seconds. The analysis tests whether there is a Stroop effect.

#This code will check if ggplot2, reshape2, pwr, and effectsize are installed.
#If not, this code will install these packages.

The Stroop effect -- the finding that it takes longer to name the font color of a word when that word names a different color (e.g., the word "red" printed in green ink) than when the word and its color match -- is one of the most robust and widely replicated phenomena in cognitive psychology [@macleod1991]. Here, we analyze a simple dataset of a Stroop experiment. Students in an introduction to psychology course completed an online Stroop task (<http://faculty.washington.edu/chudler/java/ready.html>) and named the colors in congruent trials (e.g., the word 'red' written in a red font) and in incongruent trials (e.g., the word 'red' written in a green font). The time they took to name all words was self-reported in seconds (e.g., 21.3 seconds) for both the congruent and incongruent blocks. In this analysis, we are interested in examining whether there is a Stroop effect.

All participants completed the task voluntarily as part of a classroom demonstration of research methods, and no identifying information was collected. Because no personally identifiable information was recorded and the task carried no more than minimal risk, this classroom demonstration was exempt from formal review by the Eindhoven University of Technology Ethics Review Board.
The Stroop effect is one of the largest and most consistently replicated effects in cognitive psychology [@macleod1991], so we planned our sample size assuming a conservatively large effect.

An a priori power analysis for a paired-samples *t*-test, conducted using the `pwr.t.test()` function from the `pwr` package [@champely2020], indicated that to detect a true effect of `r power_result$d` standard deviations of the difference scores, with an alpha level of `r power_result$sig.level`, and a desired power of `r power_result$power * 100`%, at least `r required_n` participants would be needed. We report data from all students who completed the task in a single course offering, exceeding this minimum.

Reaction times in the two conditions were positively correlated, *r* = `r round(cor_result$estimate, digits = 2)`, *t*(`r cor_result$parameter`) = `r round(cor_result$statistic, digits = 2)`, *p* `r format_p(cor_result$p.value)`. A dependent *t*-test indicated that based on our alpha level of 0.01 we could reject the null-hypothesis, *t*(`r round(ttest_result$parameter, digits=2)`) = `r round(ttest_result$statistic, digits=2)`, *p* `r format_p(ttest_result$p.value)`, Cohen's *d~z~* = `r round(dz_result$d_z, digits=2)`, 95% CI [`r round(dz_result$CI_low, digits=2)`, `r round(dz_result$CI_high, digits=2)`] [@lakens2013]. The students were taught in two different years, 2013 and 2014. To examine whether the Stroop effect (the reaction time in the incongruent condition minus the reaction time in the congruent condition) differed between the two cohorts, we performed a Welch's *t*-test. The Stroop effect in the 2013 cohort (*M* = `r round(year_result$estimate[1], digits = 2)`) did not differ from the Stroop effect in the 2014 cohort (*M* = `r round(year_result$estimate[2], digits = 2)`), *t*(`r round(year_result$parameter, digits = 2)`) = `r round(year_result$statistic, digits = 2)`, *p* `r format_p(year_result$p.value)`, Cohen's *d* = `r round(year_d_result$Cohens_d, digits = 2)`, 95% CI [`r round(year_d_result$CI_low, digits = 2)`, `r round(year_d_result$CI_high, digits = 2)`].
